problem: Seq2Seq VLN agents trained with teacher-forcing imitate shortest paths. This gives short trajectories, but exposure bias makes them stop early and succeed less often (they stop near the average training path length: 9.48 m vs 9.31 m GT on val-unseen). Student-forcing agents sample their own actions and succeed more often, but they learn longer, inefficient routes. Separately, the usual decoder-hidden-state-queried attention becomes unreliable once the agent drifts off the shortest path.
motivation: Both effectiveness (SR) and efficiency (SPL) matter, and each classical training regime gets only one of them. On the same CMG architecture, teacher-forcing reaches SR 0.500 with TL 9.310, while student-forcing reaches SR 0.562 with TL 13.562 on val-unseen. The authors argue a scheme that combines the two, together with a grounding module that does not depend only on the history-carrying hidden state, can get the best of both.
key_idea: Alternate teacher-forcing and student-forcing every iteration, and add a discriminator over decoder hidden-state sequences that pushes the TF and SF dynamics toward each other in both directions. Pair this with a cross-modal grounding module that adds hidden-state-free mutual text–vision co-attention to standard history-queried attention.
insight: Ablations (Table III, val-unseen) show three things. (1) Professor-forcing, which only aligns SF dynamics to TF, gives no gain over teacher-forcing (SR 0.490 vs 0.500). (2) Plain alternate learning with CMG already reaches SR 0.576 / SPL 0.491, and adding the bidirectional adversarial regularizer raises this to SR 0.593 / SPL 0.514. (3) Historical and mutual co-grounding are complementary: with AAL they reach SPL 0.483 and 0.490 alone versus 0.514 combined. Switching modes at high frequency (interval 1) is key, since SPL drops with larger intervals (shown only in a figure). The SPL gain comes mostly from higher SR, not shorter paths: the final agent's TL (12.631) stays much closer to student-forcing (13.562) than to teacher-forcing (9.310). AAL is also model-agnostic, improving Speaker-Follower by +8.3 SPL with −2.4 m TL.
method: Baseline navigator: frozen ImageNet ResNet-152 features (2048→512 via FC+ReLU) of the K navigable directions in the panoramic action space; Bi-LSTM instruction encoder (256-d word embedding, 512-d hidden); LSTM decoder (512-d); greedy decoding at inference.
Historical co-grounding: soft attention over words and panoramic views, using the previous decoder hidden state h_{t-1} as the query (as in Self-Monitoring / RCM).

Mutual co-grounding: a base vector b_t = tanh(mean visual) ⊙ tanh(mean textual) builds modality-specific queries q^x, q^v, which attend over words and views without using the decoder hidden state (co-attention in the style of Ma et al. 2018).
Action prediction: the LSTM input concatenates the 4 grounded features and the previous action embedding; logits are the inner product of W_a[h_t ⊕ x̃^h_t] with each direction's feature.

Alternate learning: training switches between teacher-forcing (NLL on GT shortest-path actions) and student-forcing (actions sampled from the policy), with a fixed curriculum and an interval of 1 iteration.

Adversarial regularizer: a discriminator (Bi-LSTM over decoder hidden states/outputs, then an MLP with FC-LeakyReLU-Dropout layers and a sigmoid) classifies TF vs SF behavior sequences. In the TF stage the generator is updated to make SF sequences look like TF; in the SF stage it makes TF sequences look like SF (bidirectional, unlike professor forcing).
Training extras: speaker-model data augmentation (Fried et al.); a variant of environmental dropout (ratio 0.4, view- and feature-level only); Adam with lr 1e-4 and batch size 64; no RL.

setting.backbone: ResNet-152 (ImageNet-pretrained, frozen features) + Bi-LSTM encoder / LSTM decoder navigator with Bi-LSTM+MLP discriminator (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: R2R train (61 scenes, 14,025 instructions) plus speaker-generated augmented instruction–path pairs (Fried et al. speaker; scale not stated). The pre-exploration variant additionally uses routes sampled from the unseen test environments with speaker-synthesized instructions.

results: On R2R, CMG-AAL reaches SR 59% / SPL 51% on val-unseen and SR 57% / SPL 50% (NE 4.61) on test without RL or large-scale pretraining. It beats EnvDrop (test SR 51 / SPL 47) and FAST, and edges AuxRN on the validation splits, though AuxRN is slightly better on test SPL (0.51 vs 0.50). With pre-exploration it reaches test SR 69 / SPL 62, above EnvDrop's 64 / 61 but with a longer TL of 11.86. As a plug-in, AAL improves Speaker-Follower from SPL 21.1 to 29.4 and Self-Monitoring from 32.7 to 35.5 on val-unseen.
limitations: Evaluated only on R2R (discrete nav-graph, LSTM-era features); there is no continuous or other-benchmark validation.
Trajectories remain long (val-unseen TL 12.631 vs 9.310 for teacher-forcing; pre-exploration TL 11.86 vs ~9.5–9.8 for baselines), so the SPL gains come mostly from SR rather than efficiency.
The text describes 'episode-wise' alternation but switches every iteration; the interval study is shown only in a figure, and baseline re-implementations differ from the originally reported numbers.
